title: Moral, not metaphysical, infallibility
source_text: CXXXVIII. Addunt gratiam efficacem in effectu suo producendo infallibilem esse, non absolute & Metaphysice, sed potius moraliter: quoniam cum sit voluntatis dispositioni maxime congrua & proportionata, voluntatem infallibiliter sed ratione admodum suavi, & voluntatis genio consentanea movet. Ad eum modum quo Homo summa egestate & inopia laborans, quamvis Physice possit centum aureos sibi oblatos respuere, tamen moraliter loquendo, positis rebus ut sunt, seu habita ratione status, conditionis, & calamitatis, eos infallibiliter acceptabit, quia sunt valde accommodati ad sublevandam illius miseriam.
pass_a_gloss: CXXXVIII. They add that efficacious grace is infallible in producing its effect, not absolutely & Metaphysically, but rather morally: since, as it is most congruous & proportioned to the disposition of the will, it moves the will infallibly but in a very gentle manner, & agreeable to the temper of the will. In the way in which a Man labouring under the utmost want & need, although Physically he can reject a hundred gold pieces offered to him, yet morally speaking, things being posited as they are, or account being had of his state, condition, & calamity, will infallibly accept them, because they are very well suited to relieving his misery.
pass_b_english: Thesis CXXXVIII. They add that efficacious grace is infallible in producing its effect not absolutely and metaphysically but rather morally. Being supremely congruous and proportioned to the will's disposition, it moves the will infallibly, yet in a very gentle way that agrees with the will's own temper.

It is like a man struggling with the direst want and poverty: physically he could turn down a hundred gold coins offered to him, but morally speaking, things being as they are, or given his state, situation and misfortune, he will infallibly accept them, because they are so well suited to relieving his distress.
